precepts.text: If the unbelieving depart, let him depart; a brother or sister is not under bondage in such cases, but God hath called us to peace. The bondage is the worldly marriage. When the spouse says I want nothing to do with that Bible and keeps the pork on one side of the stove, let them go. Those coming out of such situations have work to do before remarrying, and leadership holds the records; lean back when told to, because every backdoor marriage story is worse than the last.
precepts.point: Whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her, but the sinner shall be taken by her, because she was his portion and was meant to destroy him. Some are not made to make it; if your spirit is not girded, one of these temptations takes you.

note.label: The Divine Orchestration and Purpose of the People You Encounter

precepts.why:
Paul speaks to the same case: “But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.”

The man was wicked and inherited a wicked woman. Why? God orchestrated it, to see whether he would stay there, and to reflect what is in us so that we can change. The Lord is interested in the elect, so he puts us through trials and temptations to see if we will overcome them.

The bondage is the worldly marriage. When the spouse says, I don't care what you do, I want nothing to do with that Bible, and makes it plain and won't bend, still cooking pork and ham hocks on one side of the stove, this half is for you since you're keeping those laws, we're going to keep eating chitlins and hog maws, the house smelling like butt: if the unbelieving depart, let them depart. That is the woman of Ecclesiastes 7:26 whose heart is traps and nets, and whoso pleases God shall escape.

But those coming out of these situations have a lot of work to do before they can even think about properly marrying, and brothers and sisters are impatient. Leadership are the fathers of the men and women, and we have the records. When we tell you to lean back and let the brother or sister work on themselves, it is for a good reason, because the backdoor marriage stories are horrible, and they get worse every time a new one pops up.

precepts.text: They that use this world as not abusing it, for the fashion of this world passeth away. Use the things of the world without leaning on them over Christ; the fear should kick in on its own, so nobody has to keep checking you. Sirach 1:19, wisdom raineth down skill; walking with Christ should make you skilful in the word by default.
precepts.point: We look not at the things which are seen, which are temporal, but at the things not seen, which are eternal. America influences the whole world in music and culture, but this power will fall; the kingdom we cannot see yet lasts forever. Stack your bricks and do not be a situational Israelite.
precepts.why:
This kingdom will go down. It will pass away just like everything else. “And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.” You can use the things of this world, but do not get caught up. Do not hit the snooze button, do not abuse it, and do not lean on the things of this world over Christ.

If we really believe this Bible, we know the things of this world are going to pass away, and that fear should kick in on its own. Someone should not always have to check you. You read the Bible just like the next man. We understand young spirits, but eventually, as you walk, you check yourself.

You should become skilful in the word of God. “Wisdom raineth down skill and knowledge of understanding standing, and exalteth them to honour that hold her fast.” If wisdom is walking with you, if Christ is in you, by default you become skilful in the word and in how to apply wisdom in certain situations. You embody Christ, and everybody can see wisdom walking with you.

So the things seen are temporal and the fashion of this world passes away, while the things not seen are eternal. Use the world lightly and hold fast to wisdom.

precepts.text: If thou marry, thou hast not sinned, nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh. There will be trouble; how you handle it depends on the expectations you went in with.
precepts.point: Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord: the same way you submit to Christ and the Most High, not less and not below it. Scripture defines marriage by function, not feelings. Traditions carry meaning, but they do not replace the original design. Function first, and through aging together the feelings do what they do.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
Paul says plainly: “But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh.” Marriage is no sin, but there will be trouble in it. Every marriage meets conflict.

How a couple deals with that trouble depends on the expectations they carried into it. Scripture does not define marriage by feelings; it defines it by function. Marriage originated with God. Culture later added the ceremonies, made it a business, and put unrealistic expectations on it. The traditions may carry meaning, but they do not replace the original design. That is the modern confusion: putting feelings in front of function.

So the trouble in the flesh is expected, and it is met with the order of Ephesians 5: the husband as the head who gives himself for the wife, the wife submitting “as unto the Lord.” Marriage is meant to function first, and through aging together the feelings do what they do.

precepts.text: They that marry have not sinned, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; in marriage there will be some hard times.
precepts.point: Their arguing is the trouble in the flesh the scriptures speak of. If thou marry, thou hast not sinned, but such shall have trouble in the flesh: it is not all going to be sweet all the time. Rachel's trouble in the flesh was that she envied her sister and could not bear children, and she took it out on Jacob.

note.label: Genesis 30: Trouble in the Flesh and a Righteous Hire

precepts.why:
“But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you.” They that marry have not sinned, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; in marriage there will be some hard times. It is not all going to be sweet all the time.

Rachel and Jacob arguing is that trouble in the flesh. Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, envied her sister, and said, “Give me children, or else I die.” Jacob's anger was kindled: “Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” Jacob was not the problem; he was having no trouble producing children. Rachel's trouble in the flesh was that she envied her sister and could not bear children, and she took it out on Jacob.

precepts.text: If thou marry, thou hast not sinned; nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh.
precepts.point: Marriage is not sin, but such shall have trouble in the flesh; trials will come up in a marriage that have to be fixed with the scriptures, so ask the Most High for the mercy and the strength to endure rather than vowing what you cannot uphold.
precepts.why:
“But and if thou marry, thou hast not sinned; and if a virgin marry, she hath not sinned. Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh: but I spare you.”

Marriage is not sin, but such shall have trouble in the flesh. Trials will come up in a marriage that have to be fixed with the scriptures. That is why we do not vow on the wedding day what we cannot uphold; we ask the Most High for the mercy and the strength to endure, as Tobias prayed that they might become aged together.

precepts.text: Let every man have his own wife, and let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence, and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
precepts.point: The war laws give the same understanding: the man that had betrothed a wife and not taken her was sent back to his house, lest he die in the battle and another man take her, for the Lord is the one that goeth with the host to fight against the enemies.

note.label: Deuteronomy 24: Divorcement, Pledges, and Mercy to the Poor

precepts.why:
“Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband. Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.”

Husband and wife render due benevolence to one another; benevolence means good, it is a good thing. The year free at home to cheer up his wife is that benevolence rendered: every man with his own wife, every woman with her own husband, each giving the other what is due. Stay at home the first year and make a baby.

precepts.text: There is a difference between a wife and a virgin, the unmarried woman being the virgin who cares for the things of the Lord, not a child.
precepts.point: Fair young virgins here does not mean little girls but women of marital age, and the maiden who pleased the king would be made queen instead of Vashti, and the thing pleased the king.

note.label: Esther 2: Esther Made Queen and Mordecai Uncovers the Plot

precepts.why:
The king's servants counsel “Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king”, gathered “unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women”, and “let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti.” Fair young virgins does not mean little girls. These are women of marital age, one of whom is to be queen.

Paul shows what a virgin is in scripture: “There is difference also between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.” The virgin is the unmarried woman, set beside the wife, not a child. She is a woman who has not yet married and so careth for the things of the Lord; when she marries, she careth how she may please her husband.

So the virgins gathered to the house of the women were unmarried women, and the maiden who pleased the king became his wife and queen.

precepts.text: The married woman cares how she may please her husband, being gone from her father's house.
precepts.point: This is the woman leaving her father's house for her husband's house when we live righteously; she now cares to please her husband.

note.label: Psalm 45: Thy Throne, O God, Is Forever

precepts.why:
“Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father’s house; So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty”. This is the woman leaving her father's house for her husband's house. Corinthians shows the change: “There is difference also between a wife and a virgin. The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit: but she that is married careth for the things of the world, how she may please her husband.”

Gone from her father's house, the married woman now cares how she may please her husband, and that is when the king greatly desires her beauty, when we live righteously. “for he is thy Lord; and worship thou him.”

precepts.text: Paul urged the single life so that a man may attend upon the Most High without distraction, which is exactly what the Most High secured for Ezekiel.
precepts.point: Ezekiel spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening his wife died, and he did in the morning as he was commanded. This shows the life of a prophet, whose purpose is above family, love, and children, so when a wife or a distraction interferes with the work the Most High assigned, the purpose comes first.

note.label: Ezekiel 24: The Boiling Pot and the Sign of the Prophet's Wife

precepts.why:
Paul urged the single life: “this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction.”

Attending upon the Lord without distraction is exactly what the Most High secured for Ezekiel. He took away the desire of his eyes with a stroke, and told him to forbear to cry and make no mourning for the dead, so that the prophet went on with the work he was assigned. He spoke to the people in the morning, his wife died at even, and “I did in the morning as I was commanded.”

The purpose of a prophet is above family, love and children. When a wife or a distraction interferes with the work, the purpose comes first.

moments.label: The Art of War - Rules of Engagement

points: The eighth cause is a lack of affection and emotional connection: the husband renders due benevolence to the wife and the wife to the husband, because both need it whatever they say.
Be always ravished with her love; a lack of it in the marriage breeds anger on both sides.

note.label: The Art of War - Rules of Engagement

points: This is not a simp-out class. Do not go home, stop going to camp, stop traveling, and rub feet all day. The time is short: it remaineth that both they that have wives be as though they had none. You have to be about the Lord's business. Brothers have had a baby and been in Africa the next week. The work has to be done no matter what.

But he that is married careth for the things that are of the world, how he may please his wife. When you are not doing the work, you have to take care of your responsibilities at home, your prized possession, your pillar of rest. If you do not build her up, she is going to be a pillar of stress.

Why does it matter? Because she is teaching your kids. Do you want an unhappy, mean, angry, bitter, emotional woman bringing up your kids while you are not around? Your son is going to pick up those traits, and your daughter too. Take care of that possession at home or you will destroy it.

Sisters, how can you help? Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband. The wife hath not power of her own body. It is strange to hear of men that do not want to render due benevolence to their own wives; that one is hard to understand.

Somebody might think this class is justifying a man stepping out. No. This is how you defend your home. Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.

The scriptures say due benevolence. There are cases on both sides, but this is particularly toward the women here: do not starve your marriage, because you create that void, and the next thing you know a work husband comes in place. It brings other levels of sin, and that level of sin can go anywhere.
